definition: The Indigenous Polynesian people of Aotearoa New Zealand, and their language and culture. Māori tradition includes many iwi-specific accounts of gods, ancestors and the land, recorded in oral recitation, carving, weaving and manuscripts.

The Indigenous Polynesian people of the Hawaiian Islands, and their language and culture. Hawaiian traditions were transmitted orally and in Hawaiian-language newspapers, and they remain living practice for many communities today.
The Māori sky father, often called Rangi. He and the earth mother Papatūānuku lie together at the beginning of the world, and their separation by their son Tāne lets light into the world.
The Māori earth mother, often called Papa. She is the land itself in many understandings, and her separation from Ranginui is the origin of the world of light and of human life.
The Māori god of forests and birds, and in many accounts the creator of the first woman. He separates his parents Ranginui and Papatūānuku, and his forests are attacked by Tāwhirimātea.
A Polynesian trickster and culture hero, known in many island traditions. In Māori stories he snares the sun, fishes up the North Island, and steals fire; his deeds explain features of the world.
The Hawaiian volcano goddess, honoured especially at Kīlauea on Hawai'i Island. She is a living akua for many Hawaiians, associated with fire, lava and the shaping of the land.
A Polynesian female figure identified with the moon in some traditions and with an ancestral woman in others. Tahitian, Samoan and Hawaiian stories give her different husbands, children and endings.

A Polynesian concept of the sacred, restricted or set apart. People, places and objects can be tapu, and breaking tapu brings danger; the concept structures ritual, land and social life across Polynesia.

The Polynesian art of navigating the ocean without instruments, using stars, swells, winds, birds and clouds. Voyaging knowledge was passed down orally and is being revived by contemporary navigators and canoe traditions.
